title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Preface
This is a practical, opinionated guide to getting real work done on MedicineBow, the University of Wyoming’s flagship high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, run by the Advanced Research Computing Center (ARCC).
It is written for people joining the ASCEND engine and its ARID program — researchers doing wildfire, fire-weather, atmospheric, and geospatial modeling — but almost everything here applies to any new MedicineBow user. It assumes you are comfortable-ish on a computer but have never used a shared supercomputer before. Every chapter tries to explain why before how, because on a cluster the “why” is usually what keeps you out of trouble.

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Why this book exists
MedicineBow is a genuinely large, shared machine, and the official documentation — the ARCC wiki — is good but has gaps and, in a few places, is out of date relative to the machine as it actually runs today. The content here was written by working through onboarding on the live cluster and cross-checking every important claim against the running system in July 2026. Where the docs and the machine disagree, this book follows the machine and calls out the conflict, because a newcomer following stale docs will hit exactly those conflicts.






This is not an official ARCC document



It’s a community onboarding guide. It can drift out of date, and ARCC can change policy at any time. When in doubt, the official wiki and arcc-help@uwyo.edu are authoritative. Corrections are very welcome.

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
The shortest possible orientation
If you read nothing else, read this:

You cannot request your own account — your PI must. No project, no account. (See 2  Getting an account (your PI must do this).)
Nothing on the cluster is backed up. Not home, not project, not scratch. There are snapshots, but they live on the same array. (See 5  Where your data lives (and why nothing is backed up).)
Never run real computation on a login node. Log in, then hand work to the scheduler (Slurm) or grab an interactive session. (See 9  Why a scheduler exists.)
Every job must name your project account with --account=<project> — it’s the one directive you cannot omit. (See 10  Anatomy of a batch job.)
The partition and QOS you choose decide how long you wait and how big you can go. Short test runs and long simulations belong in different queues. This is the point of 12  Partitions and QOS on MedicineBow and 13  Queue times: which partition for what, and it’s the single most useful thing to get right early.

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
How the book is organized

Part I gets you an account and logged in.
Part II is a minimal Linux survival kit — no more than you need.
Part III covers the filesystems and moving data in and out.
Part IV covers software: modules, conda, and containers.
Part V is the heart of the book: Slurm, the batch scheduler — how to ask for resources, pick a queue, watch your jobs, run arrays, use GPUs, and survive preemption and failures.
Part VI is quick reference: a cheat sheet, troubleshooting, and a glossary.

Conventions: shell commands you type are shown in code blocks. Boxes marked Gotcha or Important are places people reliably get burned — they earned their place by actually biting someone.
Let’s get you an account.

title: 1  What a cluster is (and why your laptop isn’t one)
text:
1.1 The one-sentence mental model
MedicineBow is not “a really big computer.” It is a few hundred ordinary Linux servers (“nodes”) wired together, all mounting the same shared filesystems, all managed by a program that decides whose job runs where and when. That program is the scheduler (here, Slurm). Learning the cluster is mostly learning to work with the scheduler instead of against it.

title: 1  What a cluster is (and why your laptop isn’t one)
text:
1.2 Login nodes vs. compute nodes
There are two kinds of machines you’ll deal with, and confusing them is the most common beginner mistake.
Login nodes (mblog1, mblog2) are the front door. When you ssh in or open a terminal in the web portal, you land here. Login nodes are shared by everyone at once — dozens of people are on the same machine editing files, submitting jobs, and moving data. They are for lightweight work: editing scripts, managing files, compiling small things, submitting jobs, checking on jobs.
Compute nodes are where actual computation happens. You never SSH to them directly. Instead you ask the scheduler for one (or many), and it gives you exclusive, accounted-for access for a bounded amount of time. A compute node on MedicineBow is a serious machine — the default mb nodes have 96 CPU cores and ~1 TB of RAM each, and the GPU nodes carry up to 8 NVIDIA H100s. Your laptop has, what, 8 cores?






The cardinal sin: computing on a login node



If you run a heavy job directly on mblog1/mblog2 — a big simulation, a data-crunching Python script, a multi-hour build — you slow the machine down for everyone trying to log in and work. ARCC monitors this and will kill runaway login-node processes (and email you).
A useful rule of thumb: anything that takes more than a couple of minutes, or uses more than a core or two, belongs in a Slurm job or an interactive session — never on the login node. See Chapter 9.

title: 1  What a cluster is (and why your laptop isn’t one)
section: 1.3 Why share a machine at all?
text:
1.3 Why share a machine at all?
Because the alternative is worse. If everyone had their own dedicated server, most servers would sit idle most of the time while a few people occasionally needed far more than one server could give. Pooling the hardware and scheduling access means:

When you need 50 nodes for an ensemble, you can have them (briefly).
When you need nothing, someone else uses the hardware you’re not using.
A fair-share accounting system stops any one person from hogging everything.

The cost of this deal is that you sometimes wait in line, and you have to describe your work up front (how many cores, how much memory, how long). Most of this book is about making those two things painless.
crumbs: 1  What a cluster is (and why your laptop isn't one)

title: 1  What a cluster is (and why your laptop isn’t one)
text:
1.4 What MedicineBow is, concretely
MedicineBow is a RHEL 9 Linux cluster. Its hardware is a mix of:

General CPU nodes (the mb partition): 25 nodes, 96 cores and ~1 TB RAM each.
GPU nodes: H100, L40S, A30, A6000, and R6000 flavors — for ML, PINNs, and anything CUDA.
Absorbed older clusters: the retired Teton, Beartooth, and WildIris clusters now live on as large partitions inside MedicineBow. Teton alone is ~250 nodes.
Investor (“condo”) nodes: hardware bought by specific research groups, which the rest of us can borrow when it’s idle — with the catch that the owner can reclaim it and bump your job (see Chapter 18).

You don’t need to memorize any of this yet. The partition chapter (Chapter 12) lays out exactly which hardware to ask for, and the queue-times chapter (Chapter 13) tells you which choices leave you waiting versus running now.

2.1 The rule that surprises everyone
On many systems you sign up yourself. Not here. ARCC will not create an account without written confirmation from a Principal Investigator who owns a project. This is deliberate: accounts are tied to funded projects for accounting and fair-share purposes.
So the actual first step in your ARCC journey is a conversation, not a form:
For ASCEND/ARID performers the project is something like cowy-firesurro (the project this guide was written under). Ask your PI to confirm the exact project name — you will type it into every single job you ever run (Chapter 10), so it’s worth knowing on day one.

section: 2.4 What you get: the free tier
text:
2.4 What you get: the free tier
Each researcher’s baseline allocation:

100,000 CPU core-hours per year
20,000 GPU-hours per year

That is a lot for getting started — 100,000 core-hours is roughly one 96-core node running flat out for six weeks. Investor projects and larger allocations exist beyond this, but you almost certainly won’t hit the free-tier ceiling while you’re learning. Core-hours are counted as (cores × wall-clock hours), which is one more reason not to over-ask for resources (Chapter 11).

2.5 The practical checklist

Confirm with your PI which project you’re joining and its exact name.
Have the PI email arcc-help@uwyo.edu to request your account on that project. (You emailing them yourself won’t work — they need the PI’s confirmation.)
Once ARCC provisions you, you’ll get a UW username. Everything else in this book starts from there — your first login is Chapter 3.

No VPN is required to reach ARCC, on campus or off — so once your account exists, you can log in from anywhere.

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
text:
The web portal (Open OnDemand) is a browser interface: a file explorer, a terminal, job submission forms, and interactive apps (desktop sessions, RStudio, and — almost certainly — Jupyter). Start here on day one.
SSH is the terminal way in, and how you’ll work day-to-day once set up. It requires a key you generate through the portal first.







“Southpass” is dead — don’t use it



Older notes and search results may point you at southpass.arcc.uwyo.edu. That was the portal for the retired Beartooth cluster. The DNS name still resolves, but there’s no live service behind it for you. The current portal is medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu.

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
text:
3.2 Step 1 — Log into the portal
Go to https://medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu and sign in with your UW username and password. You’ll be prompted for Duo two-factor authentication. If you’ve never set up Duo, do it at https://wyosecure.uwyo.edu. No VPN is needed.
Once in, take the tour: there’s a Files menu (browse /home, /project, /gscratch), a Clusters → Shell option (a terminal in your browser), and an Interactive Apps menu.

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
section: 3.3 Step 2 — Generate your SSH key with the SSH Key Manager
text:
3.3 Step 2 — Generate your SSH key with the SSH Key Manager
SSH on MedicineBow is key-and-certificate based, not password based. You don’t set a password for SSH; you generate a key pair through the portal:

In the portal, open the SSH Key Manager.
Generate a key. It downloads as a zip named after your username.
Unpack it into your local ~/.ssh and fix permissions:

unzip ~/Downloads/<username>.zip -d ~/.ssh
chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh
ssh-add
Now you can connect from your own terminal:
ssh <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu






SSH keys expire after one year



This is the single best FAQ entry in the whole book. One day, roughly a year after you set up, your ssh will simply stop working — permission denied, no obvious reason. The key expired. Go back to the portal’s SSH Key Manager, generate a fresh key, unzip it into ~/.ssh again, and you’re back. Nothing is broken; it’s by design.
crumbs: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
section: 3.4 Step 3 — A comfortable SSH config (optional but worth it)
text:
3.4 Step 3 — A comfortable SSH config (optional but worth it)
Add this to ~/.ssh/config on your laptop so you can just type ssh medbow:
Host medbow
    HostName medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu
    User <username>
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ServerAliveCountMax 5
ServerAliveInterval sends a small keepalive every 60 seconds so campus/VPN firewalls don’t silently drop your connection while you’re reading output.

title: 4  The Linux you actually need
text:
4.5 Environment variables and your shell
Your shell remembers settings in variables. A few you’ll meet:
echo $HOME        # /home/<username>
echo $USER        # your username
echo $SCRATCH     # /gscratch/<username> — your scratch space
echo $PATH        # where the shell looks for commands
To make something permanent (say, a handy alias), add it to ~/.bashrc:
alias q='squeue --me'          # see just my jobs
alias proj='cd /project/cowy-firesurro'
Run source ~/.bashrc (or log out and back in) to apply changes.

title: 4  The Linux you actually need
section: 4.6 tmux: don’t let a dropped connection kill your work
text:
4.6 tmux: don’t let a dropped connection kill your work
This is the most important section in the chapter. When you SSH in and start something — even a legitimate interactive session — closing your laptop or losing WiFi kills that shell and everything running in it. tmux fixes this by keeping your session alive on the login node whether or not you’re connected.
tmux new -s work     # start a named session "work"
#   ... do things, launch an interactive job, watch output ...
#   detach with:  Ctrl-b then d
tmux ls              # list your sessions
tmux attach -t work  # reattach later, even from a different computer
The workflow that saves people:

SSH into the login node.
tmux new -s work.
Inside tmux, do your editing, submit jobs, launch an interactive session (Chapter 17).
Detach (Ctrl-b then d) and close your laptop. It all keeps running.
Tomorrow, SSH back in and tmux attach -t work — exactly where you left off.







tmux keeps login-node shells alive — batch jobs don’t need it



A submitted batch job (sbatch, Chapter 10) already runs independently of your connection — you can log out and it keeps going. tmux is for the things that live in your shell: interactive sessions, long-running monitoring, an editor you don’t want to lose.

title: 4  The Linux you actually need
text:
4.7 Permissions, briefly
You’ll occasionally see chmod and permission strings like -rw-r-----. The one you’ll actually use is fixing your SSH keys (chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh, from Chapter 3) and occasionally making a script executable:
chmod +x run.sh
There is no sudo on the cluster, ever. You can’t install system packages or change things outside your own directories — and you don’t need to. Everything you install goes in your own space (Chapter 8) or as modules (Chapter 7).
That’s the survival kit. On to where your data actually lives.

title: 5  Where your data lives (and why nothing is backed up)
text:
5.1 The single most important sentence in this book
There are snapshots (point-in-time copies you can sometimes restore from), but snapshots live on the same storage array as your live data. If that array fails, the snapshots fail with it. Snapshots protect you from “I accidentally deleted that file yesterday” — they do not protect you from hardware loss. Anything you cannot afford to lose must have a copy somewhere else (your institution’s storage, a cloud bucket, the separate Alcova service which does have real nightly backups, etc.).
Internalize this before you generate a month of simulation output onto scratch and assume it’s safe.

Check where you stand at any time:
arccquota
which prints your usage and limits for home, scratch, and project side by side.

5.2.1 /home — small, personal, for config not data
50 GB sounds like a lot until your first conda environment eats 15 GB of it. Home is for dotfiles, scripts, small configs — not datasets and not software installs. When home fills up, weird things break (jobs fail to write logs, logins misbehave), so keep an eye on it with arccquota and du -sh ~/* | sort -h.


5.2.2 /project/<proj> — the shared workhorse
5 TB, shared by everyone on your project (e.g. cowy-firesurro). This is where shared datasets, inputs, and results belong. Because it’s shared, agree on a directory convention with your group so you don’t clobber each other. It persists for 6 months after the project formally ends — long enough to get your data out, not a permanent archive.


5.2.3 /gscratch/$USER — fast and disposable
Also 5 TB, and this is the fast filesystem — use it as the working directory for running jobs that do heavy I/O. The catch is in the name: it’s scratch. Files untouched for 90 days are purged automatically. Never keep the only copy of anything here.






Is it 45 days or 90? It’s 90.



The legacy Confluence docs say scratch is purged after 45 days of inactivity. The current ARCC wiki says 90. Both pages are live on the web, which is confusing — but 90 is the current policy. Either way: don’t treat scratch as storage.




5.2.4 /lscratch — node-local, gone when the job ends
Each compute node has its own local disk mounted at /lscratch. It’s the fastest storage available to a job (no network in the way), which makes it ideal for scratch files a single job reads and rewrites constantly. But it is wiped the instant your job ends, so copy anything you want to keep back to /project or /gscratch before your job exits.
(There is no /data filesystem, despite what some docs suggest — it doesn’t exist on the machine.)

5.3 The #1 self-inflicted wound: installing software into home






Install software into /project/<proj>/software, not /home



Your project has an extra 250 GB quota specifically at /project/<proj>/software for installing software — and ARCC wants you to use it. A single conda environment with a few scientific packages can be 10–20 GB. Put two of those in your 50 GB home directory and you’re full, with mysterious failures everywhere.
Point conda, pip, R libraries, and manual builds at project software space from the start. The conda chapter (Chapter 8) shows exactly how.

title: 6  Moving data in and out
section: 6.2 Globus — the recommended path for real data
text:
6.2 Globus — the recommended path for real data
Globus transfers between “collections” (endpoints). It’s restartable, checksums what it moves, retries failures, and runs server-side — so you can start a multi-hundred-GB transfer, close your laptop, and get an email when it’s done.

Log in at https://app.globus.org (choose “University of Wyoming” as your organization, or your own institution).
Search collections for uwyo-ARCC and pick “Medicine Bow”.
The Medicine Bow collection’s root is cluster, so your project shows up at a path like /cluster/medbow/project/cowy-firesurro/....
Set the other side to your institutional or personal collection (install Globus Connect Personal on your own machine to make it an endpoint), pick files, and hit Start.







Globus needs a full UW account



ARCC-Only accounts (external collaborators — Chapter 2) cannot use Globus. If your data lives at CSU, CU, or NCAR and you’re on an ARCC-Only account, you’ll need a UW-side person to broker the transfer, or a guest collection set up for you. Sort this out before you’re blocked on a deadline.

title: 6  Moving data in and out
section: 6.3 scp and rsync — fine for small, everyday transfers
text:
6.3 scp and rsync — fine for small, everyday transfers
From your laptop, push a file up:
scp results.csv <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/cowy-firesurro/<you>/
Pull one down:
scp <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/gscratch/<you>/output.nc .
rsync is better for directories and for resuming — it only copies what changed, so an interrupted transfer picks up where it left off:
rsync -avP ./localdir/ <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/cowy-firesurro/<you>/dir/
The -P flag shows progress and enables resume; -a preserves timestamps and permissions. For anything more than a few GB, prefer Globus — a login-node scp of a huge file competes with everyone else’s login-node activity and will be slow.

title: 6  Moving data in and out
section: 6.4 rclone — cloud storage (S3, Google Drive, Box…)
text:
6.4 rclone — cloud storage (S3, Google Drive, Box…)
rclone is ARCC’s recommended CLI tool for moving data to and from cloud services. It’s a module:
module load rclone/1.63.1
rclone config          # one-time: set up a "remote" (S3 bucket, Drive, etc.)
rclone copy mydata/ myremote:bucket/path/    # copy up
rclone copy myremote:bucket/path/ ./mydata/  # copy down
rclone verifies and retries, and handles the many small-file case far better than a naive loop of scps.

title: 7  Software modules (and why module avail lies)
text:
7.1 Why modules exist
A cluster has hundreds of users who need mutually incompatible software: three versions of Python, five compilers, conflicting builds of GDAL. You can’t install all of that globally. Instead, modules let you load exactly the versions you want into your shell for this session, without affecting anyone else. Load a module and its programs appear on your PATH; unload it and they vanish.

text:
module load gcc/14.2.0        # add gcc 14 to this shell
module list                   # what do I currently have loaded?
module unload gcc/14.2.0      # remove it
module purge                  # clear everything and start clean

title: 7  Software modules (and why module avail lies)
section: 7.2 The hierarchy — the thing that confuses everyone
text:
7.2 The hierarchy — the thing that confuses everyone
MedicineBow uses Lmod in hierarchical mode. Modules are arranged in layers:

Core modules are always visible: the compilers (gcc, nvhpc-sdk, oneapi), MPI, and standalone tools.
Compiler-dependent modules — Python, R, GDAL, NetCDF, HDF5, CUDA — are hidden until you load a compiler. They were built against a specific compiler, so Lmod won’t show them until you’ve picked one.

This is why a brand-new user runs module avail, doesn’t see gdal, and concludes it isn’t installed. It is — it’s just one layer down.






Use module spider, not module avail, to answer “does X exist?”



module avail shows only what’s loadable given what you’ve already loaded — it lies by omission. module spider searches the entire tree and tells you both that something exists and what you must load first to reach it.
module spider gdal            # yes it exists; here are the versions
module spider gdal/3.13.0     # ...and exactly what to load before it


A typical geospatial stack, in order:
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0        # 1. a compiler, first
module load gdal/3.13.0       # 2. now GDAL is reachable
module load netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi
crumbs: 7  Software modules (and why `module avail` lies)

title: 7  Software modules (and why module avail lies)
text:
7.3 What’s installed (a tour)
Ask the machine for the current list with module spider, but roughly:

Compilers (core): gcc/{11.4.0, 11.5.0, 13.2.0, 14.2.0, 15.2.0}, nvhpc-sdk, oneapi, openmpi/5.0.10.
After loading a compiler: python/{3.10.6, 3.12.0, 3.14.4}, r/{4.4.0, 4.5.3}, gdal/{3.7.3, 3.13.0}, netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi, hdf5/1.14.3*, cuda-toolkit/{12.4.1, 12.6.1}, openmpi/4.1.6, rclone/1.63.1.
Standalone: apptainer/{1.3.5, 1.4.1}, singularity/4.1.0, miniconda3/24.3.0, julia/{1.10.3, 1.11.6}.







The GPU compiler contradiction



gcc/13.2.0 prints a deprecation warning telling you to move to gcc/14.2.0. But cuda-toolkit is only built against gcc/13.2.0. So GPU users have to knowingly load the “deprecated” compiler:
module load gcc/13.2.0        # yes, the one that warns you — CUDA needs it
module load cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
Ignore the warning in this case; it’s a packaging quirk, not a mistake on your part.

title: 7  Software modules (and why module avail lies)
section: 7.4 Making a set of modules load automatically
text:
7.4 Making a set of modules load automatically
Once you know the stack a project needs, save it as a named collection so you don’t retype it:
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 gdal/3.13.0 netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi
module save firestack          # remember this set as "firestack"

# next session:
module restore firestack
Prefer module restore in your submit scripts over hand-loading a long list — it’s reproducible and self-documents the environment your job needs.






Load modules in your submit script, not just interactively



The modules you load on the login node don’t automatically carry into a batch job the way you’d expect across a fresh environment. Put the module load / module restore lines inside your sbatch script so the job builds the same environment every time (Chapter 10).


When a package isn’t available as a module — or you need a pip/conda world — that’s the next chapter (Chapter 8).

text:
8.1 Conda: great, but point it away from home first
The miniconda3 module gives you conda:
By default, conda writes environments and a package cache into ~/.conda and ~/miniconda3 — i.e. straight into your 50 GB home quota. A couple of scientific environments will fill it. Fix this once, before creating any environments, by telling conda to live in your project’s 250 GB software space.
Create ~/.condarc:
Now new environments and the download cache land in project space:
Other conda notes:

module load miniconda3/24.3.0


pkgs_dirs:
  - /project/cowy-firesurro/software/<you>/conda/pkgs
envs_dirs:
  - /project/cowy-firesurro/software/<you>/conda/envs

conda create -n fire python=3.12 numpy xarray netcdf4
conda activate fire






Do this before your first conda create



If you create environments first and then set .condarc, the old ones are stranded in home and you’ll wonder why home is still full. Set .condarc on day one. If you’ve already made the mess: conda env list, remove the home-based envs, and recreate them under project space.




No mamba is installed anywhere on the cluster — use conda directly. (Recent conda is much faster than it used to be, so this is less painful than it once was.)
Activate conda inside your submit script, not just interactively, so batch jobs get the same environment (Chapter 10).

section: 8.2 Apptainer: containers for reproducibility and portability
text:
8.2 Apptainer: containers for reproducibility and portability
A container bundles an application with its entire operating-system environment into a single image file. On HPC the runtime is Apptainer (formerly Singularity) — it runs containers as you, with no root, which is why it’s the HPC-safe alternative to Docker.
module load apptainer/1.4.1

# Pull a Docker image and convert it to an Apptainer image (.sif):
apptainer pull mytool.sif docker://ghcr.io/someorg/mytool:latest

# Run something inside it:
apptainer exec mytool.sif mytool --help

# Bind your data into the container so it can see it:
apptainer exec --bind /project/cowy-firesurro:/data mytool.sif mytool /data/input.nc
Store .sif images in /project/<proj>/software — they can be large.

Situation

The software is already an Lmod module
module (Chapter 7) — least effort


Pure Python/R stack, you want to iterate
conda

You need bit-for-bit reproducibility across machines
Apptainer


A published tool ships a Docker image
Apptainer (apptainer pull docker://…)









GPUs inside containers



To use the node’s GPUs from inside a container, add the --nv flag so Apptainer exposes the NVIDIA driver: apptainer exec --nv mytool.sif .... Pair this with a GPU job (Section 17.2).

title: 9  Why a scheduler exists
text:
9.1 The tragedy of the commons, made concrete
Imagine 300 researchers and 300 nodes, and no referee. Everyone logs into whatever node looks idle and starts running. Two people land on the same node and thrash its memory until both jobs crash. Someone starts a two-week run on the node you need for a five-minute test. Nobody can tell whether a node is free or about to be. It’s chaos, and nothing finishes.
Slurm replaces “grab a node and hope” with a simple contract:
Everything in the rest of this book is really about writing that description well.

title: 9  Why a scheduler exists
text:
You describe the work: resources and a time limit.
Slurm reserves exactly that, on nodes that can provide it, and accounts for it.
Your job runs with those resources guaranteed and isolated from everyone else’s.
When your time limit is up, the job ends — which is what keeps the line moving.

title: 9  Why a scheduler exists
section: 9.2 The two ways to run work
text:
9.2 The two ways to run work
Batch jobs (sbatch) are the normal mode: you write a script that says what resources you need and what commands to run, submit it, and walk away. Slurm runs it whenever your turn comes — maybe now, maybe in an hour — and writes the output to a file. This is how you should run essentially all real computation. (Chapter 10)
Interactive jobs (salloc) give you a live shell on a compute node for when you need to poke at things by hand — debugging, exploring data, developing a script. You’re still going through the scheduler and still consuming your allocation, but you get a prompt instead of a script. (Chapter 17)
Both run on compute nodes. Neither runs on the login node — that’s the whole point (Chapter 1).

title: 9  Why a scheduler exists
section: 9.3 The three questions every job answers
text:
9.3 The three questions every job answers
Whether batch or interactive, you’re always telling Slurm three things:








Question
Directive
Covered in




Who pays? (which project)
--account
Chapter 10


How much, and how long?
--cpus-per-task, --mem, --time, …
Chapter 11


What kind of node, and how urgent?

Chapter 12



Get those right and the cluster is smooth. Get them wrong and you either wait forever, get rejected at submit time, or watch your job die halfway through. The next chapters take them one at a time.

section: 9.4 A first look at the tools
text:
9.4 A first look at the tools
You’ll meet all of these properly later, but here’s the vocabulary:
sbatch submit.sh        # submit a batch job
salloc ...              # get an interactive session
squeue --me             # what are my jobs doing?
scancel <jobid>         # cancel a job
sacct -j <jobid>        # after the fact: what happened, and how much did it use?
ARCC also ships its own friendlier wrappers — showjobreasons (“why isn’t my job running?”), showuserlimits (“what am I even allowed to ask for?”), showpartitions, sqos — which we lean on in Chapter 12 and Chapter 15.
Let’s write an actual job.

10.1 The smallest useful job
Here is a complete, working submit script. Save it as submit.sh:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro     # WHO PAYS — the one you can't omit
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00              # 10 minutes; jobs are killed at the limit
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=4G                     # always set memory explicitly (see below)
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out        # %j is replaced by the job ID

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID started at $(date)"

module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

python my_analysis.py

# Submitted batch job 123456

section: 10.2 The one directive you cannot omit
text:
10.2 The one directive you cannot omit
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro






--account is your project, not your username



Every job on MedicineBow must specify an account, and it’s the project name (cowy-firesurro), not your login name. Leave it out and the job is rejected immediately. This is the single most common first error. Confirm your exact project name with your PI (Chapter 2) and put it in every script — or set it once as a default:
# add to ~/.bashrc so you never forget it
export SBATCH_ACCOUNT=cowy-firesurro
Even so, keep --account in the script itself — it documents intent and survives being run by a collaborator whose default differs.

title: 10  Anatomy of a batch job
text:
10.4 Set memory explicitly — always






The 10 GB-per-core memory trap



On the default mb partition, if you don’t set --mem, Slurm gives you 10 GB per CPU core (DefMemPerCPU=10000). So this innocent-looking request:
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8       # and no --mem line
silently asks for 80 GB of RAM — and then you queue behind a number you never typed, because 80 GB is harder to schedule than the 8 GB you probably needed. Always set --mem (whole-job) or --mem-per-cpu explicitly. This is covered in depth in Chapter 11.

title: 10  Anatomy of a batch job
text:
10.5 Making the environment reproducible
A batch job starts in a clean-ish environment. Build the environment you need inside the script so it runs the same way every time and doesn’t depend on what you happened to have loaded when you hit submit:
module purge
module restore firestack        # a saved module set (see @sec-modules)
# or, for conda:
module load miniconda3/24.3.0
conda activate fire

title: 10  Anatomy of a batch job
text:
10.6 Useful variables inside a job
Slurm sets environment variables your script can use:
$SLURM_JOB_ID          # the job's ID
$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK   # cores you were given — pass to your program's thread count
$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID   # which array element this is (see @sec-arrays)
$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR      # the directory you ran sbatch from
A common pattern is to match your program’s threads to what Slurm gave you:
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
Now that you can submit a job, the next two chapters are about doing it well: asking for the right resources (Chapter 11), and choosing the right queue (Chapter 12).

title: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)
text:
11.1 Cores, tasks, and the words Slurm uses
Slurm’s vocabulary is a little fussy, but for most jobs you only need two ideas:
Asking for 8 cores does not make a single-threaded program faster — it just reserves 7 idle cores and makes you wait longer. Match the request to what your code can actually use.
crumbs: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)

title: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)
text:
A task is one instance of your program. Most jobs are a single task.
CPUs per task is how many cores that program can use (its threads).

#SBATCH --nodes=1                # keep a job on one node unless it's true MPI
#SBATCH --ntasks=1               # one program instance
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8        # that can use 8 cores

Single-threaded program? --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1.
Multithreaded (OpenMP, most numpy/xarray work)? --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=N, and set export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK.
MPI across many nodes? Use --nodes and --ntasks, and launch with srun (Chapter 20).
crumbs: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)

title: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)
section: 11.2 Memory — the directive people forget, then regret
text:
11.2 Memory — the directive people forget, then regret
Set memory explicitly, every time. Two ways:
#SBATCH --mem=32G              # total memory for the whole job (simplest)
# or
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G       # memory per core (scales with --cpus-per-task)






Remember the 10 GB/core default on mb



If you omit --mem on the default partition, you get 10 GB per core, so --cpus-per-task=8 silently becomes a 80 GB request. That queues slower and can be rejected outright if it exceeds a limit. Name your memory. (Full story in Chapter 10.)


How much do you actually need? For a first run, estimate high-ish so it doesn’t get killed, then measure and right-size (below). A job that exceeds its memory request is killed by the out-of-memory (OOM) killer (Chapter 19) — so memory is the one resource where running out is fatal rather than merely slow.
crumbs: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)

title: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)
section: 11.3 Time — long enough to finish, short enough to start
text:
11.3 Time — long enough to finish, short enough to start
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00        # HH:MM:SS  (or D-HH:MM:SS, e.g. 2-00:00:00)
Your job is killed the instant it hits this limit, so the request must exceed the real runtime — pad by, say, 25%. But don’t pad wildly: a shorter time limit means a lower QOS ceiling and better odds of backfilling into gaps, so it often starts sooner (Chapter 13). There’s a real tension here, and picking the time limit thoughtfully is one of the highest-leverage things you do.






There is no per-partition default time — so set --time



Partitions on MedicineBow don’t set a default wall time. If you don’t specify --time, you inherit the partition maximum (7 days), which your QOS will then likely reject (the normal QOS caps at 3 days). Always set --time yourself so the job’s request is coherent.
crumbs: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)

title: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)
text:
11.4 Over-asking punishes you first
It’s worth making this concrete, because it’s counterintuitive to newcomers:

More cores / memory → fewer nodes can satisfy you → longer wait, and you’re charged for cores you didn’t use.
More time → lower-priority QOS tier and fewer backfill opportunities → longer wait.
A GPU you don’t use → you sit in the (busy) GPU queue for nothing (Chapter 13).

The scheduler isn’t punishing you on purpose; a bigger, longer request is simply a rarer set of free resources to find. The lesson: right-size.
crumbs: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)

title: 11  Asking for resources (and why over-asking punishes you)
text:
11.5 Measure, then right-size, with seff
After a job finishes, seff tells you what it actually used versus what you reserved:
seff 123456
Job ID: 123456
State: COMPLETED
Cores: 8
CPU Efficiency: 24.13% of 04:16:00 core-walltime      <- you used ~2 of 8 cores
Memory Utilized: 5.31 GB
Memory Efficiency: 16.59% of 32.00 GB                 <- 32G reserved, 5G used
Read that as: next time ask for ~2 cores and ~8 GB. Low CPU efficiency means you reserved cores your code can’t use; low memory efficiency means you can ask for far less and start sooner. One measured run is worth a dozen guesses.
Check what you’re even allowed to ask for with ARCC’s helper:
showuserlimits
Now that you can size a job, the next decision is where to send it — partitions and QOS, and the queue-time consequences of each (Chapter 12, Chapter 13).

text:
12.1 Partition = which hardware
A partition is a named pool of nodes. Submit with --partition=<name> (the default is mb). Here’s what’s actually on the machine:
¹ One L40S node has 4 GPUs instead of 8. Numbers are the machine as observed in July 2026; verify current state with showpartitions and sinfo.
Teton, Beartooth, and WildIris are the old retired clusters, now living on as big partitions inside MedicineBow — Teton alone is ~250 nodes, which is why it swallows so much throughput work. The inv-* partitions are investor (“condo”) hardware: you can run on them when they’re idle, but the owner can reclaim the node and bump your job (Chapter 18).
You can list several partitions and let Slurm use whichever frees up first — --partition=mb,teton,beartooth is common for CPU throughput work and is exactly what the busiest jobs on the machine do.

section: 12.3 DenyOnLimit: rejected at submit, not stuck forever
text:
12.3 DenyOnLimit: rejected at submit, not stuck forever
Every QOS is flagged DenyOnLimit. If you ask for more than a QOS allows — say a 5-day run under normal (max 3 d), or more cores than the cap — Slurm rejects the job the moment you submit it, with a clear error. It does not silently queue it forever. That’s good news: you find out immediately, fix the request, and resubmit.

title: 12  Partitions and QOS on MedicineBow
section: 12.4 Putting both knobs in a script
text:
12.4 Putting both knobs in a script
#SBATCH --partition=mb          # hardware: general CPU nodes
#SBATCH --qos=fast              # tier: 12h max, high priority
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00         # within the fast 12h ceiling
For a GPU job:
#SBATCH --partition=mb-l40s
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1            # ask for 1 GPU (see @sec-gpu)
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00
Now — which combination should you actually pick? That depends entirely on whether you’re doing a quick proof-of-concept or a long production run, and how busy each queue is right now. That’s the next chapter, and it’s the one to read carefully.

title: 13  Queue times: which partition for what
text:
13.1 What the queue actually looks like right now
At a representative midday moment on MedicineBow there were roughly 2,000 jobs running and 800 pending. Almost every pending job’s reason was a single word: Priority — i.e. “the machine is busy and you’re in line,” not “you asked for something impossible.” That’s the normal state of a healthy, well-used cluster. Your job is to land in the fast-moving part of that line.

13.3 Short proof-of-concept vs. long simulation
This is the decision the whole chapter exists for.

13.3.1 Short proof-of-concept / debugging / “does it even run?”
You want to start now, run briefly, and iterate. Priority and low wait matter; walltime and footprint don’t.
#SBATCH --partition=debug        # 4 dedicated test nodes, usually idle
#SBATCH --qos=debug              # 1 h max, but starts almost instantly
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G

Use the debug partition + debug QOS for the fastest possible start on a tiny job (cap: 1 h, ≤2 nodes, ≤7 cores, ≤32 G).
Need a bit more than debug allows but still want to start fast? Use fast QOS on mb (12 h ceiling, priority 80) — median start of seconds.
Developing interactively? interactive QOS starts in ~10–30 s (Chapter 17).
For GPU proof-of-concept, develop on mb-a30 (starts in minutes), not H100.



13.3.2 Long production simulation / big ensemble / final runs
You need days of walltime and don’t want to babysit or get preempted. You accept a longer initial wait in exchange for a long, stable run.
#SBATCH --partition=non-investor   # big pool that won't be reclaimed
#SBATCH --qos=long                 # up to 7 days
#SBATCH --time=5-00:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem=32G

Use long QOS for multi-day runs (7 d ceiling). normal (3 d) is the default and fine for sub-3-day jobs.
Submit to --partition=non-investor (CPU) or non-investor-gpu (GPU) so an investor can’t reclaim your node mid-run. Or list several CPU partitions (--partition=mb,teton,beartooth) to start on whichever frees first — at the cost of possible preemption on inv-* hardware.
Checkpoint (Section 18.3). A long job is a long time to lose to a node failure, a walltime overrun, or a preemption. This is non-negotiable for production runs.
Right-size first (Chapter 11): a leaner request under long starts sooner than a bloated one.

13.4 Check the live queue before you commit
Historical medians are a guide; the machine right now is the truth. Before a big submission:
showpartitions               # idle vs busy nodes, per partition, right now
sinfo -p mb-h100 -o "%P %t %D"   # how many H100 nodes are idle this second?
gpuavail                     # ARCC helper: free GPUs by type
squeue -p mb-l40s            # how deep is the line for this partition?
showuserlimits               # what am I allowed to ask for?
If showpartitions shows two idle H100 nodes, submit now. If the GPU partitions are full and the line is long, either develop on mb-a30, or submit and walk away — but don’t sit watching an H100 queue for three hours when an A30 was free the whole time.
After a job runs, showjobreasons <jobid> explains why it’s still pending (Chapter 15) — usually Priority (just wait) or Resources (you asked for a lot).
The next chapter explains why QOS dominates your position in that line — the actual priority formula on this machine.

title: 14  How priority is actually computed here
text:
14.1 The real formula (straight from the machine)
Slurm computes a priority score for every pending job and runs the highest scores first (subject to backfill, below). The score is a weighted sum, and MedicineBow’s actual weights are:
Each factor is a number between 0 and 1, multiplied by its weight, and summed. So the biggest lever, by a wide margin, is QOS.
crumbs: 14  How priority is actually computed here

title: 14  How priority is actually computed here
text:
PriorityWeightQOS       = 200     <- dominant
PriorityWeightFairShare = 100
PriorityWeightJobSize   = 100
PriorityWeightAge       = 10
PriorityWeightPartition = 0       (partition doesn't affect priority here)
crumbs: 14  How priority is actually computed here

title: 14  How priority is actually computed here
section: 14.2 What each factor means for you
text:
14.2 What each factor means for you
QOS (weight 200) — the big one. Higher-priority QOS = dramatically better position. From Chapter 12: interactive (90) > fast (80) > normal (70) > long (60). Choosing fast over long is worth more priority than any amount of waiting will earn you. This is why the short-vs-long decision in Chapter 13 matters so much.
Fair-share (weight 100) — recent usage. Slurm tracks how much your account has used lately, relative to its share. Burn a lot this week and your fair-share factor drops, lowering priority for a while; it recovers as usage decays (half-life ~7 days here). You can’t game this — it’s the mechanism that stops any one group from monopolizing the machine. It rewards steady use over bursty hogging.
Job size (weight 100). A factor based on the resources requested. Combined with the SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME flag this cluster sets, it interacts with your time request — another reason not to over-ask (Chapter 11).
Age (weight 10) — time spent waiting. Your job slowly gains priority the longer it sits, maxing out after ~3 days. But at weight 10, age is a tie-breaker, not a strategy. You will not age your way past someone who chose a better QOS. Waiting is the weakest lever there is.
crumbs: 14  How priority is actually computed here

title: 14  How priority is actually computed here
text:
14.3 The one practical takeaway






Pick the QOS, don’t play the queue



Because QOS is weighted 2× fair-share and 20× age, the highest-leverage thing you can do for start time is choose the most appropriate high-priority QOS your job fits into — the shortest walltime tier that still lets your job finish (Chapter 13). Everything else — waiting longer, resubmitting, submitting at 3am — is noise by comparison.
crumbs: 14  How priority is actually computed here

title: 14  How priority is actually computed here
section: 14.4 Backfill: why a small job can jump the line
text:
14.4 Backfill: why a small job can jump the line
Priority decides the order, but Slurm also backfills: if the top job is waiting for, say, 40 nodes to free up, Slurm will slot in a smaller, shorter job that fits in the gap right now — as long as doing so won’t delay that top job’s reserved start time. This is why a tiny 20-minute test can start immediately even when the queue looks deep, and it’s a big part of why short jobs feel so much snappier than long ones. Requesting less time and fewer resources makes your job backfill-eligible in more gaps — yet another payoff for right-sizing.

sprio -j <jobid>            # the priority breakdown for a pending job
sprio -l                    # all pending jobs, with factor columns
showjobreasons <jobid>      # ARCC helper: plain-language "why am I waiting?"
If sprio shows your QOS factor is low because you’re on long, and the job would actually finish in 10 hours, resubmitting under fast is the single most effective change you can make.

15.5 A tiny monitoring routine
For a job you care about, this is enough:

Next: the one Slurm feature that changes how you work — job arrays.

title: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work
text:
16.1 The problem it solves
You have 500 fire-weather scenarios to run, or 500 input tiles to process. The wrong way is a bash loop that runs them one after another in a single job (serial, slow, and one crash near the end wastes everything). The other wrong way is copy-pasting 500 submit scripts. The right way is one array job: one script, submitted once, that Slurm turns into 500 independent tasks it can run in parallel and backfill wherever there’s room.
crumbs: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work

title: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work
text:
16.2 The mechanics
Add --array and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick which piece of work this task does:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --job-name=sweep
#SBATCH --array=1-500                 # 500 tasks, indices 1..500
#SBATCH --qos=fast                    # short independent tasks → high-priority QOS
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00               # per task
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/sweep-%A_%a.out # %A = array job id, %a = task index

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

# Use the task index to select this task's work:
python run_scenario.py --scenario-id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
Submit once:
mkdir -p logs
sbatch submit_array.sh        # creates 500 tasks: 12345_1, 12345_2, ... 12345_500
Each task is scheduled independently. Because they’re small and short, they backfill beautifully (Chapter 14) and the whole sweep can finish far faster than the sum of its parts.
crumbs: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work

title: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work
text:
16.3 Driving work from the index
The index is just a number; you map it to real work. Common patterns:
Line N of a parameter file:
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" params.txt)
python run.py $PARAM
The Nth input file:
FILES=(/project/cowy-firesurro/data/tiles/*.tif)
THIS=${FILES[$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID]}      # note: arrays are 0-indexed in bash
python process.py "$THIS"
(If you index files from a bash array, start --array=0; if you use sed -n Np, start --array=1. Off-by-one here is the classic array bug.)
crumbs: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work

title: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work
text:
16.4 Throttling: be a good neighbor
Don’t necessarily unleash all 500 at once — cap how many run simultaneously with %:
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20        # at most 20 tasks running at a time
This keeps you from saturating your account’s core cap (and your fair-share, Chapter 14), while still churning through all 500. A modest % limit is often faster overall because you stop competing with yourself and stay backfill-friendly.
crumbs: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work

title: 16  Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work
text:
16.5 Managing an array
squeue --me                     # shows pending tasks collapsed, e.g. 12345_[6-500]
scancel 12345                   # cancel the whole array
scancel 12345_7                 # cancel just task 7
sacct -j 12345                  # per-task outcomes after the fact
To find which tasks failed (so you can rerun only those):
sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,State,ExitCode -n | grep -v COMPLETED
then resubmit just those indices: sbatch --array=17,43,88 submit_array.sh.






Arrays vs. one big MPI job



An array is for independent tasks that don’t talk to each other (embarrassingly parallel): sweeps, ensembles, per-file pipelines. If your tasks must communicate — a single domain-decomposed simulation — that’s an MPI job instead (Chapter 20), a different tool for a different shape of problem.


Arrays are also the natural unit for ensembles in fire/atmospheric work: one array task per ensemble member, each writing to its own output, collected afterward. Reach for them early — most “I need to run this many times” problems are secretly array jobs.
Next: interactive sessions and GPUs.

title: 17  Interactive sessions and GPU jobs
text:
17.1 Interactive sessions with salloc
When you need to poke at things by hand — debug a crash, explore a dataset, build and test a model interactively — request an interactive allocation:
salloc requires at least --account and --time. When it grants the allocation you get a shell on a compute node — now you can run heavy things freely, because you’re no longer on the login node. The interactive QOS is tuned for exactly this: it starts in ~10–30 seconds (Chapter 13) with an 8-hour ceiling.
When you’re done, exit the shell to release the allocation (don’t sit on idle cores — it hurts your fair-share and blocks others).
crumbs: 17  Interactive sessions and GPU jobs

title: 17  Interactive sessions and GPU jobs
text:
salloc --account=cowy-firesurro --qos=interactive \
       --time=02:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=16G







Launch salloc from inside tmux



An interactive session lives in your shell. If your laptop sleeps or WiFi drops, the shell dies and the session ends. Start tmux on the login node first, then salloc inside it (Section 4.6). Now you can detach, close the laptop, and reattach tomorrow with the session intact — as long as it’s within your --time.




17.1.1 Interactive apps in the portal
The web portal (Chapter 3) offers graphical interactive apps — a full XFCE desktop, RStudio, and almost certainly Jupyter — that launch as scheduled jobs behind the scenes. These are the friendliest way to do interactive/GPU notebook work without wrangling salloc and port-forwarding by hand.

title: 17  Interactive sessions and GPU jobs
text:
17.2 GPU jobs
Request GPUs with --gres=gpu:<count> and target a GPU partition:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --partition=mb-l40s          # or mb-h100, mb-a30, ...
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                 # one GPU on the node
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8            # CPUs to feed the GPU
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00

module purge
module load gcc/13.2.0 cuda-toolkit/12.6.1   # CUDA needs gcc 13.2, see below
nvidia-smi                                    # confirm the GPU is visible
python train.py
To request a specific GPU type you can also use the typed form, e.g. --gres=gpu:h100:2 for two H100s on one node.

Don’t develop on H100s



H100 nodes are the most contended resource on the machine — waits of several hours are normal when they’re busy (Chapter 13). Do your iterate-fast development on A30s, which you can usually get in minutes, and only submit to mb-h100 when you have a real training run that needs that horsepower. Check gpuavail and showpartitions before choosing.








The GPU compiler quirk



cuda-toolkit is built only against gcc/13.2.0, even though gcc/13.2.0 prints a deprecation warning nudging you to gcc/14.2.0. For GPU/CUDA work, load gcc/13.2.0 anyway and ignore the warning (Chapter 7). Inside containers, add --nv to expose the GPU (Chapter 8).

gpuavail                    # ARCC helper: free GPUs by type, right now
slurm_gpustat               # cluster-wide GPU utilization
sinfo -p mb-h100 -o "%P %t %G %D"   # H100 node states this second
nvidia-smi                  # inside a GPU job: is my code actually using the GPU?
nvtop                       # inside a GPU job: live GPU usage, like htop for GPUs
If nvidia-smi shows 0% utilization while your job runs, your code isn’t actually on the GPU — a common and expensive mistake. Verify early.

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
18.1 The condo model, plainly
A lot of MedicineBow’s hardware was purchased by individual research groups. Those inv-* partitions “belong” to their investors, who get top priority (QOS 110) on them. To keep the machine busy, everyone else’s jobs can backfill onto idle investor nodes — free capacity, most of the time.
The deal has a string attached:
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
An investor can reclaim their node and requeue your job



If you land on investor hardware and the owner submits work, your job is preempted — Slurm kills it and (by default here) requeues it: it goes back into the pending queue to start over from the beginning when resources free up. Any progress not written to disk is lost. This can happen minutes into a job or days in. For a long, un-checkpointed simulation, that’s potentially days of wasted compute.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
section: 18.2 Two ways to protect a long run
text:
18.2 Two ways to protect a long run
1. Run where you can’t be preempted. Submit long production jobs to the non-preemptible pool:
#SBATCH --partition=non-investor        # 110 CPU nodes, not reclaimable
# or non-investor-gpu for GPU work
This is the correct home for anything long that you haven’t checkpointed. (The --constraint=non-investor some docs mention does not work — it’s a partition, not a constraint. See Chapter 12.)
2. Checkpoint, so preemption is cheap. If you do run on borrowable hardware (or list several partitions for faster starts), make preemption survivable by saving state periodically.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
18.3 Checkpointing
A checkpoint is a periodic save of enough state to resume rather than restart. It protects you from three things at once: preemption, node failures, and hitting your walltime limit. Any job measured in days should checkpoint.
The pattern:

Every so often (every N iterations, or every ~30–60 min of wall time), write current state to a checkpoint file in /gscratch or /project — not /lscratch, which is wiped when the job ends (Chapter 5).
On startup, check for a checkpoint and resume from it if present, otherwise start fresh.
Write checkpoints atomically (write to a temp file, then rename) so a crash mid-write can’t corrupt your only checkpoint. Keep the last one or two.

Many scientific codes have this built in — WRF has restart files, PyTorch has torch.save/load for model+optimizer state, PETSc and Sundials have checkpoint hooks. Turn these on and set the interval to your risk tolerance.
Auto-resubmit on requeue. Combine checkpointing with a self-resubmitting job so a preempted or timed-out job comes back automatically:
#SBATCH --requeue                          # allow this job to be requeued
#SBATCH --open-mode=append                 # don't clobber the log on requeue
#SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@120                # send USR1 120s before the walltime kill

# resume from checkpoint if one exists
if [ -f state.ckpt ]; then
    ./simulate --restart state.ckpt
else
    ./simulate --fresh
fi
The --signal line asks Slurm to warn your script 120 seconds before it’s killed for walltime; trap that signal to flush a final checkpoint before you go.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
18.4 Requeue behavior worth knowing

A requeued job keeps its job ID but starts its command from the beginning — Slurm doesn’t magically resume your program; your checkpoint does.
--open-mode=append stops the requeued run from overwriting the previous log.
Check whether a job was requeued with sacct -j <id> --format=JobID,State,Start,End — you’ll see multiple rows.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
18.5 The one-line policy






If a job runs longer than a few hours, checkpoint it



Short jobs (minutes to an hour or two) can just be rerun if something goes wrong — don’t over-engineer them. But any multi-hour or multi-day job should checkpoint, and any long production run should also prefer non-investor. The combination — non-preemptible partition and checkpoints — is what lets big simulations finish reliably on a shared, condo-model machine.


Next: reading the wreckage when a job fails outright.

title: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage
text:
19.2 Out of memory
The most common surprise. A job that exceeds its memory reservation is killed instantly by the Linux OOM killer — you’ll see OUT_OF_MEMORY in sacct, and often a truncated or empty output file.
sacct -j 123456 --format=JobID,State,MaxRSS,ReqMem
# MaxRSS is peak memory actually used; compare to ReqMem
If MaxRSS is near (or above) ReqMem, raise --mem and resubmit. Then use seff (Chapter 15) on the successful run to right-size going forward. Remember the 10 GB/core default trap on mb (Chapter 11) — sometimes the fix is realizing you did have enough memory and something else was wrong.
crumbs: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage

title: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage
text:
19.3 Timeout
TIMEOUT means your job was still running when the clock ran out and Slurm killed it. Options, in order of preference:

Checkpoint so the next run resumes instead of restarting (Section 18.3). This is the durable fix for genuinely long work.
Raise --time — but staying under your QOS ceiling (normal = 3 d, long = 7 d), and knowing a longer request may wait longer to start (Chapter 13).
Make the job finish faster — more cores if it scales, or a smaller problem per job (an array, Chapter 16).
crumbs: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage

title: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage
text:
19.4 Your program crashed (FAILED)
FAILED with a non-zero exit code is usually your code, not the cluster. Read the output:
cat slurm-123456.out          # stdout+stderr (or separate --error file)
Common culprits on a cluster specifically:

Module not loaded in the script. Interactive worked, batch didn’t — because you loaded modules on the login node but not inside the submit script. Put module load in the script (Chapter 10).
Wrong paths. A relative path that existed where you ran sbatch but not where the job ran. Use absolute paths or $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR.
conda env not activated in the script (Chapter 8).
Wrote to /lscratch and it vanished — that’s node-local and wiped at job end (Chapter 5).

title: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage
text:
19.5 Node failure and preemption
NODE_FAIL (hardware died) and PREEMPTED/REQUEUED (investor reclaimed the node, Chapter 18) aren’t your fault and aren’t your bug. The response is the same: checkpoint so a restart is cheap, run long jobs on non-investor, and add --requeue so they come back automatically. If node failures recur on the same node, report it to arcc-help@uwyo.edu with the job ID.
crumbs: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage

title: 19  When jobs fail: reading the wreckage
text:
19.6 A debugging loop that works

sacct -j <id> ... → get the State. That narrows it to one of the four families above.
If resource-related (OOM/timeout) → adjust --mem/--time, resubmit.
If FAILED → read slurm-<id>.out, fix the code/env, and reproduce it fast in a debug-QOS job (near-instant start, Chapter 13) rather than waiting in a long queue each iteration.
Once it works, seff <id> → right-size → promote to the real partition/QOS.

Using the debug partition as your fast edit-run-debug loop, and only graduating to big queues once the job is known-good, will save you more time than any other habit on the machine.
That’s the operational core. Part VI is quick reference you’ll come back to.

title: 20  The parallelism ladder
text:
20.1 Climb only as high as you need
Newcomers often reach straight for MPI or GPUs because they sound like “real HPC.” Usually the right answer is much lower on the ladder and far simpler. Match the rung to the shape of your problem.

title: 20  The parallelism ladder
text:
20.1.1 Rung 1 — Serial
One core, one task. Perfectly fine for small jobs, and the right baseline: get it correct on one core first. If a serial job is fast enough, you’re done — don’t parallelize for sport.
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1


20.1.2 Rung 2 — Job array (many independent serial runs)
If you need to run the same thing many times over different inputs — a parameter sweep, an ensemble, per-file processing — this is almost always the answer. It’s the biggest bang for the least complexity, and it backfills beautifully (Chapter 16).
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20
python run.py --id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
Reach here first whenever the phrase “I need to run it N times” applies.


20.1.3 Rung 3 — Multicore (one program, many threads, one node)
If a single run is too slow and your code is multithreaded (OpenMP, or numpy/xarray/PyTorch using many cores), give it more cores on one node:
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
./my_threaded_program
Only ask for as many cores as your code actually scales to — check with seff afterward (Chapter 11). Doubling cores rarely doubles speed.


20.1.4 Rung 4 — MPI (one program across many nodes)
When a single problem is too big for one node — a domain-decomposed simulation like WRF, where pieces must exchange data every step — you need MPI. This is genuine distributed computing: one program, many processes across many nodes, communicating.
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks=384                 # e.g. 96 tasks/node × 4 nodes
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 openmpi/5.0.10
srun ./my_mpi_simulation             # srun launches the MPI ranks
Use srun (not mpirun) to launch — it’s integrated with Slurm and gets the task layout right automatically. MPI is powerful but a real step up in complexity; only climb here when a problem genuinely won’t fit on one node. For long MPI runs, prefer non-investor and checkpoint (Chapter 18).


20.1.5 Rung 5 — GPU
For workloads built for GPUs — deep learning, PINNs, some CFD/linear algebra — a GPU can beat dozens of CPU cores. But only if your code actually targets the GPU (Section 17.2); a CPU program gains nothing from a GPU node except a longer queue. Develop on mb-a30, scale up to mb-h100 for real training (Chapter 13).
#SBATCH --partition=mb-a30
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
module load gcc/13.2.0 cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
python train.py

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.1 Login and access
A symptom-first index to the rest of the book.
“Permission denied (publickey)” when I ssh — it worked before. Your SSH key almost certainly expired (they last one year). Regenerate it in the portal’s SSH Key Manager, unzip into ~/.ssh, chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh (Chapter 3).
“Permission denied” on a brand-new setup. Check permissions: chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh, and make sure you unzipped the key into ~/.ssh. Confirm you’re using medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu, not the dead southpass name.
I can’t get an account at all. Only a PI can request it, in writing, against a project. You cannot self-register (Chapter 2).
Globus won’t let me add the collection. If you’re an external collaborator on an ARCC-Only account, you can’t use Globus. You need a UW-side guest collection (Chapter 6).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.2 Jobs won’t submit
sbatch: error: ... You have to specify an account. Add --account=cowy-firesurro (Chapter 10).
Job violates accounting/QOS policy (...) at submit time. Your request exceeds a QOS limit (every QOS is DenyOnLimit). Usually --time exceeds the QOS ceiling — e.g. 5 days under normal (max 3 d). Lower --time or switch QOS (Chapter 12). Check ceilings with sqos and showuserlimits.
Invalid qos specification. Your account can’t use that QOS. Yours are debug, fast, interactive, long, normal (sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=qos).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.3 Jobs won’t start
Stuck in PENDING with reason Priority. The machine is just busy and you’re in line. Either wait, or pick a higher-priority (shorter) QOS — QOS dominates priority here (Chapter 14). Small/short jobs backfill sooner.
Stuck with reason Resources. You asked for a lot (many cores, much memory, a scarce GPU). Right-size (Chapter 11), or accept the wait. showjobreasons <id> explains in plain language.
GPU job pending for hours. H100/L40S are heavily contended (Chapter 13). Develop on mb-a30 instead, and check gpuavail/showpartitions for what’s actually free before submitting.
Pending with QOSMax... or AssocGrpCpuLimit. You (or your account) hit a cap — e.g. too many cores in flight at once. Wait for your other jobs to finish, or throttle an array with % (Chapter 16).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.4 Jobs fail
OUT_OF_MEMORY. Raise --mem. Compare MaxRSS to ReqMem in sacct (Chapter 19). Watch the 10 GB/core default trap (Chapter 11).
TIMEOUT. Job outran --time. Checkpoint (Section 18.3), raise --time within the QOS ceiling, or split the work into an array.
FAILED, worked interactively but not in batch. You loaded modules / activated conda on the login node but not inside the submit script. Put them in the script (Chapter 10, Chapter 8).
Output file references files that “don’t exist.” Relative paths from the wrong directory, or you wrote to /lscratch (wiped at job end). Use absolute paths or $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR; copy /lscratch output out before the job ends (Chapter 5).
PREEMPTED / REQUEUED on a long job. You were on investor hardware and got reclaimed. Move to --partition=non-investor and checkpoint (Chapter 18).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.5 Software
“That module doesn’t exist” but I’m sure it does. module avail only shows what’s reachable now. Use module spider <name> — you probably need to load a compiler first (Chapter 7).
CUDA won’t build / link. Load gcc/13.2.0 (not 14) — cuda-toolkit is built against 13.2 despite its deprecation warning (Chapter 7).
Home directory full, everything breaking. Conda in /home. Move envs to /project/<proj>/software via ~/.condarc, and clean up (Chapter 8). Check with du -sh ~/* | sort -h.
GPU job runs but is slow / nvidia-smi shows 0%. Your code isn’t actually on the GPU. Verify the framework sees CUDA; in a container, you need --nv (Section 17.2).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.6 Still stuck?
Email arcc-help@uwyo.edu with your job ID, the submit script, and the error. Or bring it to office hours, Tuesdays 11am–1pm on Zoom. Include what you already tried — it gets you a faster answer.

title: 23  Glossary
text:
Plain-language definitions of the terms this book uses.

Account (Slurm)

The project that a job is charged to (e.g. cowy-firesurro). Required on every job via --account. Not your username. See Chapter 10.

ARCC

Advanced Research Computing Center — the UW group that runs MedicineBow.

ASCEND / ARID

The NSF Regional Innovation Engine (ASCEND) and its wildfire-resilience program (ARID) that many readers of this book work under. See the preface.

Backfill

Slurm slotting a small, short job into a gap in the schedule without delaying higher-priority jobs. Why short jobs start fast. See Chapter 14.

Batch job

A job submitted as a script with sbatch that runs unattended when scheduled. The normal way to run work. See Chapter 10.

Checkpoint

A periodic save of a job’s state so it can resume instead of restart after a preemption, timeout, or crash. Essential for long jobs. See Section 18.3.

Compute node

A machine where computation actually runs, allocated to you by Slurm. Distinct from a login node. See Chapter 1.

Condo model

The funding model where research groups buy nodes (inv-*) and others borrow them when idle, subject to reclaim/preemption. See Chapter 18.

Core-hour

One CPU core used for one hour — the unit your allocation is measured in. Reserving 8 cores for 1 hour costs 8 core-hours whether or not you use them.

DenyOnLimit

A QOS flag meaning an over-limit request is rejected at submit time, not silently queued. See Chapter 12.

Fair-share

A priority factor reflecting your account’s recent usage relative to its share; heavy recent use temporarily lowers your priority. See Chapter 14.

GRES (Generic RESource)

How you request GPUs: --gres=gpu:1 or --gres=gpu:h100:2. See Section 17.2.

Investor / inv-*

Nodes/partitions owned by a specific group, who get top priority; others can be preempted off them. See Chapter 18.

Job array

One script run many times with a varying index ($SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID), for parameter sweeps and ensembles. Max 10,000 tasks. See Chapter 16.

Lmod / module

The system that loads specific software versions into your shell on demand. Hierarchical: many modules are hidden until you load a compiler. Use module spider. See Chapter 7.

Login node

The shared front-end machine (mblog1, mblog2) you land on when you connect. For editing and submitting — not for computing. See Chapter 1.

MedicineBow

UW/ARCC’s current flagship HPC cluster. The subject of this book.

MPI

Message Passing Interface — the standard for a single parallel program spanning many cores or nodes that communicate. Launched with srun. Contrast with job arrays. See Chapter 20.

OnDemand (Open OnDemand)

The web portal at medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu — file browser, terminal, and interactive apps. See Chapter 3.

OOM (Out Of Memory)

When a job exceeds its memory reservation and is killed. Fix by raising --mem. See Chapter 19.

Partition

A named pool of nodes with particular hardware (mb, mb-h100, teton, non-investor, …). Chosen with --partition. See Chapter 12.

Preemption

An investor reclaiming a borrowed node, causing your job to be killed and (here) requeued. See Chapter 18.

Priority

The score that orders pending jobs. On MedicineBow it’s dominated by QOS (weight 200). See Chapter 14.

QOS (Quality of Service)

The service tier that sets your max walltime, resource cap, and priority (debug, fast, normal, long, …). The most important scheduling choice you make. See Chapter 12.

Requeue

Putting a killed (preempted/failed) job back in the pending queue to start over. Pair with checkpointing. See Chapter 18.

Scratch (/gscratch, $SCRATCH)

Fast, large, temporary storage purged after 90 days of inactivity. Not backed up. See Chapter 5.

seff

A command showing a finished job’s CPU and memory efficiency — use it to right-size. See Chapter 15.

Slurm

The scheduler that manages all jobs on the cluster. The thing you’re really learning to use. See Chapter 9.

Snapshot

A point-in-time copy of a filesystem, on the same array as the live data. Protects against accidental deletion, not hardware loss. Not a backup. See Chapter 5.

Walltime

Real elapsed clock time a job is allowed (--time). The job is killed at the limit. See Chapter 11.
